## Setup

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be **symmetric**, i.e. $A^\top = A$. We write the
standard inner product as $\langle x, y\rangle = x^\top y$. Symmetry is equivalent to
self-adjointness:

$$
\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle \qquad \text{for all } x,y \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$ {#eq-selfadjoint}

The whole theorem flows from @eq-selfadjoint.

## The result

::: {#thm-spectral}

## Spectral Theorem

If $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is symmetric, then there exist an orthogonal matrix
$Q$ (so $Q^\top Q = I$) and a real diagonal matrix $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$
such that
$$
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top .
$$ {#eq-decomp}
Equivalently, $\mathbb{R}^n$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $A$, and every
eigenvalue is real.

:::

We build to it with two lemmas.

::: {#lem-real}

## Eigenvalues are real

Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric $A$ is real.

:::

::: {.proof}
Let $Ax = \lambda x$ with $x \neq 0$, allowing complex $\lambda, x$. Using the conjugate
transpose $x^*$ and $A^\top = A$ with real entries,
$$
\lambda \,\langle x, x\rangle = x^* A x = (A x)^* x \big/ \ \cdots\ = \bar\lambda\, \langle x, x\rangle .
$$
Since $\langle x,x\rangle = \|x\|^2 > 0$, we get $\lambda = \bar\lambda$, so $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$. $\qquad\blacksquare$
:::

::: {#lem-orthogonal}

## Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal

If $Ax = \lambda x$ and $Ay = \mu y$ with $\lambda \neq \mu$, then $\langle x, y\rangle = 0$.

:::

::: {.proof}
By @eq-selfadjoint,
$$
\lambda \langle x, y\rangle = \langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle = \mu \langle x, y\rangle,
$$
so $(\lambda - \mu)\langle x, y\rangle = 0$. As $\lambda \neq \mu$, $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$. $\qquad\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}

## Proof of @thm-spectral (sketch)

Induct on $n$. The base case $n=1$ is immediate. For the step, @lem-real gives a real
eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ with unit eigenvector $q_1$. Its orthogonal complement
$q_1^\perp$ is $A$-invariant (by @eq-selfadjoint), so $A$ restricts to a symmetric
operator on an $(n-1)$-dimensional space. The inductive hypothesis supplies an
orthonormal eigenbasis there; adjoining $q_1$ yields an orthonormal eigenbasis of
$\mathbb{R}^n$. Collecting these vectors as columns of $Q$ gives @eq-decomp. $\qquad\blacksquare$
:::

A complete treatment, including the self-adjoint operator version on Hilbert spaces,
is in @rudin1991functional; for the numerical side see @trefethen1997numerical.

## Numerical check

Decompositions should be tested, not trusted. We build a random symmetric matrix,
diagonalize it, and confirm @eq-decomp holds to machine precision.

::: {#fig-spectral .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 6
M = rng.standard_normal((n, n))
A = (M + M.T) / 2                      # symmetrize

eigvals, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)         # eigh exploits symmetry
Lambda = np.diag(eigvals)

reconstruction_error = np.linalg.norm(A - Q @ Lambda @ Q.T)
orthogonality_error  = np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ Q - np.eye(n))

print(f"eigenvalues (all real): {np.round(eigvals, 4)}")
print(f"|A - Q Λ Qᵀ|  = {reconstruction_error:.2e}")
print(f"|QᵀQ - I|     = {orthogonality_error:.2e}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
eigenvalues (all real): [-2.0037 -0.988   0.2761  0.4913  1.5001  1.8151]
|A - Q Λ Qᵀ|  = 1.62e-15
|QᵀQ - I|     = 1.39e-15
```
:::
:::


Both residuals sit near $10^{-15}$, confirming the decomposition numerically.

## Takeaways

- Symmetry $\Rightarrow$ self-adjointness (@eq-selfadjoint) is the engine of the whole proof.
- Real eigenvalues (@lem-real) and orthogonality (@lem-orthogonal) are the two ingredients.
- In practice, call a symmetry-aware routine like `eigh`, not the general `eig`.
